title: The issues technique: capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
blurb: Walk any issue through the five steps of the issue management technique and say who acts at each one.
question: An issue has been identified and its impact on scope needs to be understood. In which step of the issue management technique does that happen, and what comes next?

teach.body: The PRINCE2 7 issue management technique has five steps: capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement. The manual's headings are capturing issues, assessing issues, recommending resolution, deciding on changes and implementing changes. In plain English: write it down, work out what it means for the project, set out the options, let the right person choose, then carry out the choice and update the records.

steps.label: Capture
steps.sub: determine type and severity; register it

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: impact on business case, targets, risk profile

teach.caption: The issue register in the project log sits beneath every step.

teach.body: Issues can be captured through any formal or informal channel. Capturing means determining the issue type and its severity or priority, then registering it. Assessing answers two questions: does this issue affect the project, and if so, how? Look at the impact on approved targets and tolerances, the business case, other products or work packages, and the risk profile, and recheck severity. Assessment works best cooperatively, drawing on team members and stakeholders.

Based on the assessment, options are identified and evaluated, and a recommendation goes to the person or group with the required authority, making clear the consequences of approving and of rejecting. The decision maker escalates anything beyond their delegated authority. Typical decisions are to approve, reject, ask for an exception plan or request more information; for an off-specification, a concession may be granted.

root.label: Is it within the decision maker's delegated authority?

children.label: Decide
children.sub: approve, reject or request more information

teach.h: Who usually acts at each step
head: Step
Usually done by
rows: Board, change authority, or PM within authority
teach.caption: In the processes, this runs through controlling a stage: capture issues and risks, take corrective action, escalate issues and risks.

teach.body: Once a decision is made, corrective action is taken, usually through new or amended work packages, and records are updated. Approved requests for change and off-specifications are recorded in the project log and reflected in the affected management products and the baseline. Each system holding baselines should provide a record of changes and an archive of superseded versions. The issue is closed once it has been considered and the change implemented.

At Quayside Logistics, team manager Dev Patel reports that the new handheld scanners cannot read older pallet labels. Project manager Marta Kowalski captures it as a problem with high priority and registers it. Assessing it with Dev and the warehouse supervisors, she finds a two-week delay but no breach of stage tolerance. She evaluates relabelling versus a software patch and recommends the patch. It is within her delegated authority, so she approves it and issues an amended work package.

teach.text: Classic traps: options are recommended only AFTER assessment, and the person who recommends is not necessarily the person who decides. Do not confuse this technique with the risk technique (identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate).

items: Five steps: capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement.
Capture: determine type and severity or priority, then register.
Assess: does it affect the project, and how? Targets, tolerances, business case, other products, risk profile.
Recommend: identify and evaluate options; show the consequences of approving and rejecting.
Decide: escalate if beyond authority; approve, reject, ask for an exception plan or request more information.
Implement: corrective action; update records, management products and the baseline.

summary: You can now walk an issue through capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement, saying what happens and who usually acts at each step. You can also name the typical decisions and explain when an issue must be escalated.

A.q: In the issue management technique, which step comes immediately after 'assess'?
options: Decide
Recommend
Implement
Capture
A.why: The order is capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement (manual 10.3.1).

whyNot.0: A decision follows a recommendation, which in turn follows assessment.
whyNot.2: Implementation is the last step, after a decision.
whyNot.3: Capture is the first step, before assessment.

A.q: In which step of the issue management technique are the issue type and its severity or priority first determined?
options: Capture
Assess
Recommend
Decide
A.why: Capturing an issue means determining its type and its severity or priority, then registering it.

whyNot.1: Assessment rechecks severity and priority, but they are first determined at capture.
whyNot.2: Recommending is about identifying and evaluating options.
whyNot.3: Deciding is about choosing a course of action within authority.

A.q: Which question does the assess step aim to answer?
options: Who raised this issue, and through which channel?
Which team should build the products affected?
What lessons can be passed to future projects?
Does this issue affect the project, and if so how?
A.why: When assessing issues, the aim is to answer whether the issue affects the project and, if so, how (manual 10.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: The source and channel are noted when capturing; they are not the aim of assessment.
whyNot.1: Allocating work happens later through work packages when a change is implemented.
whyNot.2: Lessons are captured through the progress practice and the lessons log.

B.q:
Which two statements about the issue management technique are correct?
1. Options are identified and evaluated before a recommendation is made.
2. The project manager decides on every request for change once it is assessed.
3. Assessing issues works best cooperatively, using input from team members and stakeholders.
4. Changes are implemented before the decision so that time is not lost.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Options are evaluated before a recommendation (1), and assessment is best done cooperatively (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: decisions are made by whoever holds the required authority, which may be the board or a change authority.
whyNot.2: Both are false: the PM decides within delegated authority, and implementation follows the decision.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: implementation is the last step, after the decision.

B.q: What should a recommendation make clear to the person or group with the required authority?
options: The names of everyone who raised the issue
The risk appetite set by the business layer
The consequences of approving and of rejecting
The lessons from earlier, similar projects
B.why: Whether the recommendation is to approve or reject, the consequences of both choices should be made clear (manual 10.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Who raised the issue is recorded at capture; it is not what the recommendation must clarify.
whyNot.1: Risk appetite is set by the business and used for risk tolerances, not for issue recommendations.
whyNot.3: Lessons may inform options, but the recommendation must set out the consequences of the choices.

B.q: Which is a typical decision option at the decide step?
options: Transfer the issue to a third party
Exploit the issue to make it certain
Accept the issue as a project risk
Ask for an exception plan
B.why: Typical decisions are to approve, reject, ask for an exception plan or request more information (tab 10.1).

whyNot.0: Transfer is a risk response for threats, not an issue decision.
whyNot.1: Exploit is a risk response for opportunities.
whyNot.2: An issue has already happened or is certain, so it is not turned into a risk.

C.q: A request for change has been assessed and options set out, but it is beyond the project manager's delegated authority. Which step is this, and what happens?
options: Recommend; the PM approves it and informs the board later
Implement; the team manager builds it, then reports it
Decide; it is escalated to those with the authority
Capture; it is logged in the risk register for review
C.why: At the decide step, anything beyond delegated authority is escalated to the person or group with the required authority.

whyNot.0: The PM cannot approve beyond delegated authority, and recommending is not deciding.
whyNot.1: Nothing is implemented until a decision has been made.
whyNot.3: The request has already been captured and assessed, and issues go in the issue register.

C.q: During a stage, a new issue must be registered. Which technique step and which controlling a stage activity cover this?
options: Capture; capture issues and risks
Assess; evaluate stage status
Decide; give ongoing direction
Implement; take corrective action
C.why: Registering a new issue is part of the capture step, carried out in the controlling a stage activity 'capture issues and risks'.

whyNot.1: Evaluating stage status compares actual progress with the plan; registering a new issue is capture.
whyNot.2: Give ongoing direction is a directing a project activity for the board, not a controlling a stage activity.
whyNot.3: Corrective action follows a decision; it does not register a new issue.

C.q: After a change has been approved, what does the implement step involve?
options: Reassessing the business case and closing the project log
Taking corrective action and updating records and the baseline
Asking the board for an exception plan before work restarts
Raising a fresh request for change for each affected product
C.why: Implementing means taking corrective action and updating the project log, the affected management products and the baseline (manual 10.3.1.5).

whyNot.0: The project log is closed in closing a project, not when one change is implemented.
whyNot.2: Asking for an exception plan is a decision option, not part of implementing an approved change.
whyNot.3: The change has already been approved; implementation carries it out rather than raising new requests.

reteach.title: The leaking roof
reteach.question: How would a school business manager deal with a leaking classroom roof using the five steps?

blocks.body: Capture: the caretaker reports the leak, and it is logged as urgent. Assess: does it affect lessons, and how badly? Recommend: a patch now or a new roof section, with the costs and consequences of each. Decide: the patch is within the manager's budget, but a new roof needs the governors. Implement: the roofer is booked and the maintenance log updated.

blocks.text: Recommending is not deciding. If the choice is beyond your authority, you recommend and escalate.

explain.body: Capturing, assessing and recommending are usually done by the project manager, helped by project support. The decision may sit elsewhere.

test.q: Who usually carries out the capture, assess and recommend steps?
options: The project board, with project assurance
The team manager, with the developers
The business layer, with the executive
The project manager, with project support
test.why: Steps 1 to 3 are usually carried out by the project manager, assisted by project support.

whyNot.0: The board decides on escalated issues; it does not usually do the groundwork.
whyNot.1: Team managers raise issues and implement corrective actions in work packages.
whyNot.2: The business layer sits outside the project management team.

explain.body: Typical decisions on an issue: approve, reject, ask for an exception plan, or request more information. For an off-specification, a concession may be granted.

test.q: Which list contains decision options from the decide step?
options: Approve, reject or request more information
Avoid, reduce, transfer or accept the issue
Plan, do, check or act on the issue
Exploit, enhance or share the issue
test.why: Approve, reject and request more information are typical decisions, alongside asking for an exception plan.

whyNot.1: Avoid, reduce, transfer and accept are threat responses in the risk practice.
whyNot.2: Plan, do, check, act is the cycle behind the progress practice.
whyNot.3: Exploit, enhance and share are opportunity responses in the risk practice.

explain.body: If an issue needs a decision beyond the decision maker's delegated authority, it is escalated to the next level up. If it would take the stage beyond tolerance, the PM raises an exception report.

test.q: During the decide step, an issue is found to be beyond the decision maker's delegated authority. What should happen?
options: It is recorded as a lesson and then closed
It is turned into a risk for later monitoring
It is escalated to the next level of authority
It is passed to a team manager to resolve
test.why: The decide step escalates anything beyond delegated authority to whoever holds the required authority.

whyNot.0: Closing an undecided issue leaves its impact unmanaged; it must be escalated.
whyNot.1: It is already an issue; changing its label does not give anyone authority to decide.
whyNot.3: Team managers work within their work package; they do not hold more authority than the decision maker.

explain.body: Implementing means corrective action plus updating the project log, the affected management products and, where needed, the baseline, keeping old versions archived.

test.q: Which activity belongs to the implement step?
options: Determining the issue type and its severity
Updating affected products and the baseline
Identifying and evaluating the possible options
Checking the impact on the project risk profile
test.why: The implement step includes updating the records, the affected management products and the baseline (manual 10.3.1.5).

whyNot.0: Type and severity are determined at capture.
whyNot.2: Options are identified and evaluated at the recommend step.
whyNot.3: Impact on the risk profile is checked at the assess step.
